name: Arabic (Modern Standard)
variety: Modern Standard Arabic read aloud in formal, fully vocalised style by an educated speaker of Levantine background, the norm of Thelwall & Sa'adeddin (1990). Stress in words without a heavy syllable, the value of jīm, voice onset time and intonation follow the colloquial background of the speaker; where figures come from a colloquial variety this is said.
sources: Thelwall, Robin & Sa'adeddin, M. Akram (1990). Arabic. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 20(2): 37-39. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 1999.
Al-Ani, Salman H. (1970). Arabic Phonology: An Acoustical and Physiological Investigation. The Hague: Mouton.
Watson, Janet C. E. (2002). The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic. Oxford University Press.
Jongman, Allard, Herd, Wendy, Al-Masri, Mohammad, Sereno, Joan & Combest, Sonja (2011). Acoustics and perception of emphasis in Urban Jordanian Arabic. Journal of Phonetics 39: 85-95.
Davis, Stuart (1995). Emphasis spread in Arabic and Grounded Phonology. Linguistic Inquiry 26: 465-498.
Card, Elizabeth (1983). A phonetic and phonological study of Arabic emphasis. PhD dissertation, Cornell University.
Yeni-Komshian, Grace H., Caramazza, Alfonso & Preston, Malcolm S. (1977). A study of voicing in Lebanese Arabic. Journal of Phonetics 5: 35-48.
Alghamdi, Mansour (2006). Voice print: voice onset time as a model. Arab Journal for Security Studies and Training 21(42): 89-118 (in Arabic). Values taken from the summary in AlDahri (2013).
AlDahri, Sulaiman S. (2013). A study for the effect of the emphaticness and language and dialect for voice onset time (VOT) in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). arXiv:1305.2680.

Kelly, Niamh E. & Keshishian, Lara (2021). Voicing patterns in stops among heritage speakers of Western Armenian in Lebanon and the US. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 44: 103-129 (review of Arabic voice onset time studies).
Khattab, Ghada & Al-Tamimi, Jalal (2014). Geminate timing in Lebanese Arabic: the relationship between phonetic timing and phonological structure. Laboratory Phonology 5(2): 231-269.
de Jong, Kenneth & Zawaydeh, Bushra Adnan (1999). Stress, duration, and intonation in Arabic word-level prosody. Journal of Phonetics 27: 3-22.
Chahal, Dana & Hellmuth, Sam (2014). The intonation of Lebanese and Egyptian Arabic. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing. Oxford University Press.
Ghazali, Salem, Hamdi, Rym & Barkat, Melissa (2002). Speech rhythm variation in Arabic dialects. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2002, Aix-en-Provence.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (one Iraqi speaker of Standard Arabic, vowels spoken in isolation)
vowel_formants.notes: Arrays are F1, F2, F3 in Hz. The third formant is given by the source for /a/ and /aː/ only; it is null where not reported. These are plain (non-emphatic) vowels. Next to emphatic consonants F2 of /a/ falls by 200-300 Hz or more and F1 rises.

contrasts: emphatic (pharyngealised, retracted tongue root) against plain coronals: tˤ dˤ sˤ ðˤ against t d s ð
vowel length: three short and three long vowels
consonant gemination for every consonant, word-medially and word-finally
pharyngeal /ħ ʕ/ against glottal /h ʔ/ against post-velar /x ɣ/
interdental fricatives /θ ð ðˤ/ against sibilants /s z sˤ/
voicing in obstruents (there is no /p/ and no /v/ in native words)
allophony: /a/ and /aː/ are front [æ]~[a] in plain surroundings, back [ɑ] next to the emphatics /tˤ dˤ sˤ ðˤ/ and usually next to /q x ɣ/ and /r/; word-final /a/ is centralised [ɐ]
/i iː/ are retracted and lowered towards [ɨ]~[ɪ] before emphatic and pharyngeal consonants; /u uː/ are lowered towards [ʊ]~[o] in the same surroundings

emphasis spreads from an emphatic consonant to the sounds of the preceding and following syllables of the word; only /j/ (and in colloquial varieties also /i/ and /ʃ/, for rightward spread) blocks it; leftward spread is the stronger and reaches the start of the word

acoustically emphasis raises F1, lowers F2 and raises F3 of neighbouring vowels, by the same amount before and after the consonant; the effect lasts through the whole vowel for /a/ and fades quickly in /i/ and /u/ (Jongman et al. 2011); Card (1983) measured an F2 lowering of 200-300 Hz
/t k/ are aspirated, /tˤ/ and /q/ are unaspirated; voiced stops have voicing lead
/ʕ/ is a pharyngealised glottal stop or pharyngeal approximant with creaky voice, not a true fricative; /ħ/ is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative
/x/ is post-velar to uvular with uvular trilling [χ]; /ɣ/ is [ɣ]~[ʁ]
/r/ is an alveolar trill, a single tap between vowels in fluent speech, a full trill when geminate; it backs a neighbouring /a/ unless /i/ is adjacent
/l/ is clear [l]; emphatic [ɫ] occurs only in the name Allāh after /a/ or /u/
jīm is [dʒ] in the reference variety, [ʒ] in much of the Levant and the Maghreb, [ɡ] in Egypt
the /l/ of the definite article assimilates completely to a following coronal consonant (sun letters), giving a geminate
in pause the final short vowels and nunation are dropped and tāʾ marbūṭa is [a]; long vowels shorten in closed syllables and word-finally
a word-final geminate before pause is released with a short schwa-like offglide
syllable_structure: CV, CVː, CVC; CVːC and CVCC word-finally in pause; CVːC word-internally before a geminate
phonotactics: every syllable has exactly one onset consonant; words written with an initial vowel begin with a glottal stop
no word-initial consonant clusters: a prosthetic vowel with hamzat al-waṣl precedes them and is dropped in connected speech
all consonants may be geminate, and a long vowel may precede a geminate (/maːdda/)
consonants of the same place of articulation avoid each other within a root

stress.rule: Stress falls on the final syllable if it is superheavy (CVːC or CVCC, mostly pausal forms), otherwise on the penult if it is heavy (CVː or CVC), otherwise on the antepenult; suffixes added to the word are disregarded in the Levantine tradition and words of light syllables only follow the speaker's colloquial pattern (Egyptian readers say madˈrasa, Levantine readers ˈmadrasa).
stress.cues: duration and intensity, with a rising pitch accent on the stressed syllable of accented words; stressed vowels are longer and less centralised (de Jong & Zawaydeh 1999)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in careful Standard Arabic; unstressed short vowels shorten and centralise slightly, and colloquial varieties (most of all the Maghrebi ones) delete them
rhythm.notes: Ghazali, Hamdi & Barkat (2002) place the Arabic dialects in the stress-timed group, the eastern dialects with a higher vocalic proportion than the western ones. Quantity must be kept: a short vowel or single consonant must never reach the duration of a long one.

length.notes: Long vowels are about twice as long as short ones: 100-150 ms against 225-350 ms in connected words (Al-Ani 1970); 80 ms against 145 ms, ratio 1.8, in Jordanian CVC words (Jongman et al. 2011); ratio about 1 to 2.1 in Lebanese Arabic (Khattab & Al-Tamimi 2014). Geminates are about twice as long as single consonants and the vowel before a geminate is a little shorter. Vowel length is neutralised word-finally.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: t, k, tˤ: Alghamdi 2006 (Saudi speakers) as reported by AlDahri 2013; d: studies of Najdi, Qatari and Lebanese Arabic reviewed by Kelly & Keshishian 2021, which give -75, -69 and -67 ms
voice_onset_time_ms.notes: Values depend strongly on the dialect. Lebanese Arabic has shorter lags (t 20-30 ms depending on the vowel, d -40 to -70 ms: Yeni-Komshian et al. 1977 as reported by Kelly & Keshishian 2021), Najdi Arabic longer ones (t 68.5 ms). In Jordanian Arabic the interval from burst to vowel onset is 16 ms for emphatic stops and 27 ms for plain ones (Jongman et al. 2011).

intonation.declarative: a rising pitch accent on the stressed syllable of nearly every content word, the peaks stepping down through the phrase, and a final fall to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of a statement, with or without the particles hal or ʔa; the accents are as in a statement but in a raised register and the last word ends in a rise to a high boundary
intonation.wh_question: highest peak on the question word, then a falling contour to a low boundary
intonation.continuation: high phrase boundary or rise at the end of each non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: L+H*: low at the start of the stressed syllable, peak late in it or just after it
intonation.notes: The intonation of Standard Arabic is that of the speaker's colloquial variety. The description follows Egyptian and Lebanese Arabic (Chahal & Hellmuth 2014); Egyptian Arabic puts a pitch accent on every content word.

phonation: pharyngealisation with retracted tongue root as a secondary articulation of /tˤ dˤ sˤ ðˤ/ and of the vowels around them
no contrastive phonation type on vowels

problems: The emphatic consonants are not pharyngealised: ط is the plain dental phoneme t[ (IPA t̪), ص is s[ (IPA s̪), ظ (phoneme Z) uses the formant data of plain ð and has the IPA name ð, and ض (dH) has the transitions of plain d. The contrast is carried only by the following vowel.

Emphasis colouring reaches only the vowel directly after ص ض ط ظ (rules with the letter group F choose the vowels a. i. u.). The vowel before an emphatic stays plain (first vowel of بَطَل and مَطَر) and no other syllable is affected, against the spread over the word described in the literature.
No back [ɑ] next to q, x, ɣ or r, and no emphatic [ɫ] in الله.
Text without vowel signs gets no short vowels and no gemination unless the word is in ar_listx (about 30,000 entries): يكتبون gives [jktbuːna].

When the vowel sign comes before the shadda (the Unicode canonical order) the .replace rule in ar_rules corrupts the sequence to two shaddas and the vowel after the geminate is lost: كَتَّبَ gives kat:b'a and مَرَّة gives m'aRRt. The order shadda then vowel works.

Stress does not follow syllable weight. The default is the antepenultimate vowel (stressRule 4 in the voice file), a final closed syllable with a short vowel forces penultimate stress (rules with =), and every word that begins with ب ف ك ل و has its first syllable marked unstressed as if it were a proclitic. So long vowels do not attract stress: جَمِيل gives ˈdʒamiːl, يَكْتُبُونَ gives jakˈtubuːna, الصَّبَاح is stressed on its second syllable; and كَتَبَ gives kaˈtaba, مَدْرَسَة gives madˈrasat.
The diphthong /aj/ is two vowels with the stress on the second: بَيْت gives [baˈit] and سَيْف gives [saˈif].
Case endings and tāʾ marbūṭa are always spoken as written (مَدْرَسَة ends in [at]); there are no pausal forms.
/ʕ/ (phoneme A) is built from rhotic formants with aspiration noise, and غ is sent to the velar phoneme Q although a phoneme gH is defined in ph_arabic.
No language-specific intonation: the default tunes are used.
good: ħ, ʕ, χ, q and ʔ are separate phonemes
long vowels (the : phoneme adds length) and geminates from shadda are rendered, so quantity contrasts are audible
the article assimilates to sun letters
backed vowel variants exist for the position after an emphatic
a large vocalised word list (ar_listx) covers frequent unvocalised words

notes: For synthesis the emphatics need their own cue on both neighbouring vowels: lower F2 and higher F1 at the vowel edge next to the consonant, strongest for /a/. The plain voiceless stops need aspiration, the emphatic /tˤ/ and /q/ none.
